name: GLPK
workload: LP solve time: relative total solution time of GLPK, lp_solve, Clp and HiGHS on the HiGHS group's LP test set (INFORMS 2019 slides), and ALGLIB's benchmark over 90 NETLIB LP problems.
claimed_speedup: HiGHS-team slides (INFORMS 2019), relative time, lower is better: Clp 1.4, HiGHS 5.4, GLPK 28, lp_solve 108, so GLPK is about 3.9x faster than lp_solve (derived from page data). ALGLIB NETLIB benchmark: leaders (ALGLIB, HiGHS, Clp) similar, GLPK roughly 2x behind them, lp_solve roughly 3x behind, so GLPK about 1.5x faster than lp_solve (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: GNU package; 57 stars on an archived 4.60 snapshot (github.com/firedrakeproject/glpk), not the official repo
tradeoffs: Simplex (primal and dual), interior point and branch-and-cut MIP in plain C with the GNU MathProg modelling language and glpsol CLI; single-threaded; GPL (not LGPL), so linking forces GPL on the combined work.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: the numbers come from WebSearch result summaries because webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk, alglib.net and the other pages are blocked from this sandbox (ENOTFOUND); the slide table, test set, hardware and solver versions were not seen. The same sources rank GLPK well behind the current open-source leaders (Clp 1.4 and HiGHS 5.4 against GLPK 28 on the slides, about 20x and 5x; ALGLIB: GLPK about 2x behind the leaders); a Sandia 2013 comparison also found GLPK could not match Clp's speed (snippet only). So the only win is over lp_solve, the slowest solver in those sets, and the HiGHS slides are by a competing solver's authors. An unverified Medium post claims GLPK beats Clp and HiGHS on a few large LPs (woodw, pilot, pds-20). The GLPK FAQ's claim of being faster than lp_solve 4.0 'in many cases' has no numbers and is old. repo_url is the project page from the lead list, not opened (gnu.org ENOTFOUND); the only GitHub copy found (firedrakeproject/glpk) is an archived single-commit 4.60 snapshot, so last_commit and maintenance are unknown. Category sparse-and-solvers chosen over the lead's guessed blas-lapack because GLPK is an LP/MIP solver.

name: GMP
workload: Boost.Multiprecision's integer algorithm suite (random operands of 128 to 16384 bits, totals in seconds, 500000 operations per cell except where the suite uses fewer for powm and gcd) with the gmp_int backend (GMP mpz_t) against the tommath_int (LibTomMath) and cpp_int (Boost header-only) backends; plus its Miller-Rabin real-world test (1000 random 128-bit numbers tested for primality).
claimed_speedup: Only rows where the relative scores match the bracketed times are quoted. powm at 1024 bits: gmp_int 5.14976 s, tommath_int 12.628 s (2.45x slower, relative 2.45216), cpp_int 46.9932 s (9.13x slower, relative 9.12533); powm at 512 bits: gmp_int 0.766677 s, tommath_int 3.21051 s (4.19x), cpp_int 9.06469 s (11.8x). gcd at 2048 bits: gmp_int 8.18516 s, cpp_int 17.7583 s (2.17x), tommath_int 42.8729 s (5.24x). Multiplication at 1024 bits: gmp_int 0.100546 s, cpp_int 0.224062 s (2.23x), tommath_int 0.168568 s (1.68x). Decimal string conversion at 2048 bits: gmp_int 0.00244981 s, cpp_int 0.0137593 s (5.6x), tommath_int 0.202054 s (82x). Miller-Rabin real-world test: mpz_int 0.00466034 s, tom_int 0.0226395 s (4.9x, derived from page data), cpp_int 0.0497465 s (10.7x, derived from page data); the page says GMP's modular exponentiation is about 5x faster than cpp_int's. The suite's text calls GMP/MPIR, MPFR and MPC 'the world's fastest implementations generally agreed'.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ 10.3.0; optimisation flags not stated in the docs; GMP 6.2.0, Boost 1.78.0 (107800), run date Sep 30 2021
stars_or_usage: Reference arbitrary-precision integer library; widely packaged (Alpine gmp 6.3.0-r2); Boost.Multiprecision calls it the speed benchmark for big numbers
tradeoffs: C API with caller-managed mpz_t memory (plus the gmpxx C++ wrapper); hand-written assembly kernels per CPU family; heap allocation per integer dominates at small sizes; mpz functions are not constant-time (mpn_sec_* exist), so do not use for secret-dependent crypto; LGPLv3/GPLv2 dual licence.
caveats: Third-party suite (Boost.Multiprecision docs, written by a different project) with public benchmark code, but CPU model and compiler flags are not stated, which is why this is B rather than A. The relative-score column is inconsistent with the bracketed times in some cells (for example gcd at 4096 bits has both gmp_int 18.7879 s and cpp_int 32.2572 s marked 1, and at 16384 bits cpp_int is marked best although its time is 201.791 s against gmp_int 122.14 s), so only consistent rows are quoted. GMP is not fastest everywhere in the same suite: cpp_int(fixed) beats it on small fixed-width multiplication (128-bit * : 0.00116759 s vs 0.00560549 s), and in the Boost.Polygon Voronoi real-world test mpz_int took 0.103619 s against 0.0270196 s for int256_t and 0.0487904 s for cpp_int because of allocation (3.8x and 2.1x slower). Numbers are for GMP behind Boost's gmp_int wrapper, not raw mpz_t. FLINT's own pages claim 2-10x over GMP in many cases (snippet only), so GMP is the incumbent rather than the unconditional winner. repo_url is the project site from the lead list; gmplib.org was not reachable from this sandbox (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so licence comes from a package record (Alpine) and last_commit is unknown. The lead's guessed category fft is wrong; GMP is an arbitrary-precision integer library.

name: GNU MPFR
workload: Boost.Multiprecision float algorithm suite (500000 operations per cell, 50, 100 and 500 bit mantissas) with the mpfr_float backend against cpp_bin_float, cpp_dec_float and GMP mpf (gmp_float), plus its real-world tests that run all of Boost.Math's Bessel-function and non-central-T test cases at 50 digits.
claimed_speedup: Multiplication at 500 bits: mpfr_float 0.321884 s, cpp_bin_float 0.850904 s (2.64x slower, derived from page data), cpp_dec_float 1.6902 s (5.25x). Division at 500 bits: mpfr_float 1.2162 s, cpp_bin_float 5.32129 s (4.38x, relative 12.3684 vs 2.82683), cpp_dec_float 22.744 s (18.7x). Multiplication at 50 bits: mpfr_float 0.0161758 s, cpp_bin_float 0.0720574 s (4.45x), cpp_dec_float 0.061884 s (3.83x). Real-world Bessel tests (50 digits): mpfr_float_50 0.115838 s, cpp_bin_float_50 0.207745 s (1.79x, derived), cpp_dec_float_50 0.422285 s (3.65x, derived). Non-central T (50 digits): mpfr_float_50 19.1749 s, cpp_bin_float_50 38.5842 s (2.01x, derived), cpp_dec_float_50 77.9505 s (4.07x, derived). The page text says the header-only backends are 'significantly slower than the world's fastest implementations generally agreed to be found in GMP/MPIR, MPFR and MPC' and that factors of about two through five are observed at a few hundred to several thousand digits.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ 10.3.0; optimisation flags not stated in the docs; GMP 6.2.0, MPFR version number 262146 (4.0.2), Boost 1.78.0 (107800), run date Sep 30 2021
stars_or_usage: Reference correctly-rounded arbitrary-precision float library; MPFR 4.2.2 released 2025-03-20 per the project history page seen in search results; dependency of GCC and many CAS systems
tradeoffs: Built on GMP; every operation is correctly rounded with explicit rounding modes and exponent-range handling, which costs time against GMP's mpf; C API with caller-managed mpfr_t; LGPLv3+; no thread-safe global state beyond documented caches.
caveats: Third-party suite (Boost.Multiprecision docs), public code, but CPU model and compiler flags missing, so B not A. Against the lead's guessed baseline GMP it is NOT faster: in the same tables GMP's mpf (gmp_float) beats mpfr_float on most operations (500-bit division 0.430233 s vs 1.2162 s, 2.8x; 500-bit addition 0.0273382 s vs 0.0609463 s, 2.2x; 500-bit multiplication 0.292919 s vs 0.321884 s) and in both real-world tests (Bessel 0.0959515 s vs 0.115838 s; non-central T 17.2475 s vs 19.1749 s), so MPFR's advantage is over Boost's own header-only backends only, and mpf does not guarantee correct rounding. mpfr_float construction is 5-25x slower than cpp_bin_float's (50 bits: 0.0773304 s vs 0.0030982 s). At 50-100 bits cpp_dec_float is close to mpfr on addition and subtraction. Wrapped by Boost's mpfr_float, not raw mpfr_t. repo_url is the project site (www.mpfr.org seen only in search results; mpfr.loria.fr and gitlab.inria.fr ENOTFOUND), licence from an Alpine package record; last_commit unknown. The lead's category fft is wrong.

name: GSL
workload: Gamma-variate generation in samples per second, GSL against Boost.Random's gamma_distribution, reported in Boost trac ticket 6135 before and after a patch to Boost's algorithm.
claimed_speedup: GSL about 22.3 million samples/s against Boost 5.4 million (Boost was using Knuth's method), about 4.1x (derived from page data); after the patch Boost reached about 14.5 million samples/s, leaving GSL about 1.5x faster (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: GNU package; 639 stars on github.com/ampl/gsl, a CMake/AMPL-bindings copy of the latest stable release
tradeoffs: Plain C library with dozens of generators (gsl_rng) and distributions; global error-handler and abort-on-error defaults; GPL (not LGPL), which restricts use in proprietary code; not a performance-tuned library in its linear algebra (reference-style CBLAS).
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: the figures come from a WebSearch summary of Boost trac ticket 6135; trac.cpp.al is blocked from this sandbox (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the ticket text, compiler, hardware and Boost version were not seen (the ticket is about 11 years old). The win is largely a defect in Boost's old gamma sampler, since fixed; the patched gap is about 1.5x and no current Boost versus GSL measurement was found. In other snippets GSL does not win: a 2012 Rcpp Gallery post timed GSL's Mersenne Twister Gaussian draws slower than R's rnorm and Armadillo; S. Gerlach's PRNG slides reportedly say GSL is faster for Gaussian sampling than C++11, Boost and TRNG, but no numbers were visible. Boost.Math's performance tests also treat GSL as a comparison target for special functions (GSL 2.5 beta ratio about 3.14 slower than Boost, tentative). No evidence was found for GSL beating a BLAS/LAPACK or FFT incumbent (the lead's guessed category fft is wrong). repo_url is the project page from the lead list (gnu.org ENOTFOUND); the GitHub copy github.com/ampl/gsl was opened (GPL-3.0, 288 commits, no date shown), last_commit unknown.

name: htslib
baseline: Samtools 0.1.19 (the original libbam-based implementation HTSlib grew out of)
workload: BAM read-write loop and BAM to SAM conversion using 16 threads, HTSlib-based samtools against Samtools 0.1.19, as reported in the HTSlib paper abstract (GigaScience 2021).
claimed_speedup: BAM read-write loop running 5 times faster and BAM to SAM conversion 13 times faster (both using 16 threads, compared to Samtools 0.1.19).
stars_or_usage: 953 stars; core library of samtools and bcftools; downloaded more than 1 million times from GitHub and conda and used directly by an estimated 900 GitHub projects (paper abstract)
tradeoffs: C library for SAM, BAM, CRAM, VCF and BCF with BGZF thread pools, CSI/BAI/TBI indexes, optional libdeflate, libcurl, bzip2 and xz; depends only on zlib in the minimal build; MIT/Expat outside cram/, 3-clause BSD inside cram/; wrapped from Perl, Python, Rust and R.
caveats: The peer-reviewed paper (Bonfield et al., GigaScience 2021, giab007) is the source; its full text, hardware, compiler and per-tool tables (HTSlib versus HTSJDK 2.22.0, Sambamba 0.7.1 and Scramble 1.14.13 at HTSlib 1.10.2) were not reachable (PMC, bioRxiv, OUP and eprints.gla.ac.uk all ENOTFOUND), so only the abstract, which appears in the repo README as a BibTeX entry, is quoted. The baseline is HTSlib's own predecessor, not an independent competitor, and the 16-thread setting means part of the gain is better use of threading rather than per-core speed. Project NEWS also says libdeflate makes compression 'twice as fast and decompression faster' than zlib, with 'results vary by CPU' and no method. The CRAM benchmark page at htslib.org/benchmarks/CRAM.html was not reachable. The lead's guessed category big-integer-arbitrary-precision is wrong; genomics-file-formats is not one of wave 8's seven categories, so it may need re-filing.
